## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The project leads open with the posture they say runs through all ten entries: *"Stop trying to build a model that cannot be fooled."* [V] Instead, "Build the system around it, so that when the model is fooled, and it will be, nothing important breaks." [V] (p. 5) [AR]. For the first time the practitioner vote that built every earlier version was tested against a record of what has gone wrong: a corpus of 7,714 real incidents from public vulnerability databases and an AI-harm database, with classifiers that placed "the 6,639 that carried enough detail to sort" [V] (p. 5) [AP]. The question was "Does what practitioners fear match what the incident record shows?" [V]; the answer was not always, and the leads say the disagreements "taught us more than the agreements did" [V] (p. 5) [AR].

The vote carries three-quarters of the weight and the incident data a quarter: enough to move an entry a tier where belief and evidence diverge widely, not enough to let imperfect data rewrite the list (p. 5) [AR]. Prompt injection stays first although the raw incident record drops it out of the top 10; the leads read that gap as "a defense effect" (p. 5) [AR]. Misinformation runs the other way: voters placed it near the bottom, the record near the top, and the list seats it in the middle (p. 5) [AR]. Excessive Agency climbed to third, and the list's scope stops where the model becomes an actor with tools, memory and downstream consequences, at which point the risk moves to the OWASP Agentic Top 10 (p. 7) [AR].

Across the entries the same posture recurs as engineering guidance. Prompt injection is "intrinsic to current generative AI" [V], so defense is architectural: constrain what the model may do and what its outputs may reach (LLM01, p. 13) [AR]. Authorization belongs in deterministic logic outside the model (LLM03, p. 25; LLM08, p. 48) [AR]; hidden context should be assumed discoverable (LLM08, p. 46) [AR]; model output is to be treated as coming from any other user, under a zero-trust approach (LLM10, p. 56) [AR]; misinformation is "a system-level failure" [V] because outputs now drive actions (LLM07, p. 43) [AR]. Appendix A consolidates the ten entries' mappings to nine external frameworks, replacing the per-entry framework sections (p. 58) [AP].

## Part I: Front matter: method and what changed (pp. 1–9)

### License and Usage; Revision History (p. 2)

The document is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0: free to share and adapt for any purpose, even commercially, under the attribution and ShareAlike terms, with no additional restrictions; it is not legal advice, and links to third-party sites are for convenience, without OWASP endorsement (p. 2) [AP]. The revision history lists Version 1.0 (2023-08-01), Version 1.1 (2023-10-16), Version 2025 (2024-11-18), and Version 2026 with its date left as "[2026 release date]" (p. 2) [AP].

### Letter from the Project Leads (p. 5)

Every earlier version was built on judgment: hundreds of practitioners weighed in on what matters most, and that vote remains "the spine of the list" [V] (p. 5) [AP]. This year the project pulled together the 7,714-incident corpus, built classifiers to place the 6,639 sortable incidents, and asked whether fear and record match (p. 5) [AP]. The vote and the data "parted ways in specific, useful places" [V] (p. 5) [AR].

*Prompt injection.* Practitioners rank it first; ranked by the raw incident record it falls out of the top 10 entirely. "That gap is a defense effect." [V] Teams fight injection hard, so fewer clean exploits reach a public database, and the public count understates the risk mature teams already spend real money holding off. The surface sits everywhere a model reads untrusted input, so it stays first, and since that surface cannot be closed, teams build for the day it is used against them (p. 5) [AR].

*Misinformation.* The leads ask readers to "slow down on" [V] this entry. Voters placed it near the bottom; the incident record placed it near the top, "the widest gap in the direction that actually hurts" [V], where the vote sits low and the evidence high. The list seats it in the middle: the vote holds the greater weight, but the evidence pulled it up. "The disagreement is the point." [V] When fluent, confident output drives a decision or a tool call, a wrong answer becomes a wrong action, and the record says that failure lands more often than the vote assumes (p. 5) [AR].

*Weighting.* The community vote carries three-quarters of the weight; the incident data covers the remaining quarter, deliberately. "This list is a consensus product, and one noisy year of data does not get to overturn the judgment of the people doing the work." [V] A quarter weight can move an entry a tier when the belief–evidence gap runs wide, but cannot let imperfect data rewrite the list on its own; that balance decided every final slot (p. 5) [AR].

### What's New in the 2026 Top 10 (pp. 6–7)

Figure 1 is captioned as the rank migration from the 2025 to the final 2026 list, colour-coded by movement: steady, escalated, deprioritized, or renamed/re-scoped (p. 6) [AP]. The prose says the order moved more than in past years, tracking the gap between belief and evidence (p. 7) [AR]:

- Excessive Agency climbed to third, "the most consequential move on the list" [V], because vote and record agree that agentic deployments are where the damage is landing (p. 7) [AR].
- Unbounded Consumption rose four places, carried by practitioners who weigh resource and cost exhaustion higher than its old rank (p. 7) [AP].
- Improper Output Handling fell the furthest, from fifth to tenth (p. 7) [AP].
- Prompt Injection held the top spot on the strength of the vote and the defense effect (p. 7) [AP].
- Sensitive Information Disclosure held second, "the one place at the top where belief and evidence simply agree" [V], where the project's confidence is highest (p. 7) [AP].
- System Prompt Leakage is now Hidden Context Exposure, "a broader framework for the same failure to trust information that should have stayed out of reach" [V] (p. 7) [AP].

Several entries grew by absorbing newer risks instead of becoming new categories: "Standing up thin new categories would have splintered the list for no gain." [V] (p. 7) [AR]. Prompt Injection now covers cross-modal attacks that hide instructions in an image or audio track; Supply Chain covers the trust failure when a promoted model artifact is not what it claims to be; Data and Model Poisoning absorbs fine-tuning subversion; Improper Output Handling spans the insecure code assistants generate at scale (p. 7) [AP].

*The component–actor boundary.* "This list owns the risk when the model is a component inside your application." [V] Once the model becomes an actor, with tools it can call, memory it carries between sessions, and consequences it sets in motion downstream, the risk moves to the OWASP Agentic Top 10. Many of the incidents the project read sit on that boundary; readers should use an entry here for the model-as-component failure and pair it with the Agentic list once the model acts on its own, since "neither one covers that ground alone" [V] (p. 7) [AR].

### Moving Forward (p. 8)

"You can trust this list and act on it today." [V] It combines the judgment of practitioners who attack and defend these systems with the record of what has gone wrong, each checked against the other, a grounding that "is what earlier versions could only promise" [V] (p. 8) [AR]. The leads' instruction: "Work all ten, start at the top, and build each of them for the day the model is turned against you." [V] Doing so covers both what the field fears most and what it has already been burned by (p. 8) [AR]. The list is a community product shaped by developers, data scientists and security practitioners who brought their judgment and, this year, their incident records (p. 8) [AP]. Signed Steve Wilson, Project Lead, and Rock Lambros, Co-Lead (p. 8).

### LLM Top 10 at a Glance (p. 9)

Figure 2's caption describes the attack surface as a bullseye: entry vectors on the perimeter converge through amplifying machinery to three core impacts, and not every LLM04 attack flows inward, since some deliver impact directly (p. 9) [AP]. The figure itself was not inspected (text-only scope).

## Part II: The ten risk entries

### LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection (pp. 10–17)

**Description.** A prompt-injection vulnerability occurs when input to an LLM (direct user input, retrieved content, tool output, image, audio or video, intermediate reasoning, or persistent memory) alters the model's behavior in ways the developer did not intend (p. 10) [AP]. LLMs make no architectural distinction between instructions and data, both being tokens on one stream, so there is no clean equivalent to parameterized queries (NCSC, 2025) (p. 10) [BT]. Inputs need not be human-readable, need not come directly from a user, and need not be visible in the rendered interface (p. 10) [AP].

Three deployment-time properties make it worse (p. 10) [AR]: *context-window pooling*, where system prompt, user input, retrieved documents, tool outputs, history and memory form one token stream with no enforced trust boundary; *memory persistence*, where an injection written to long-term memory, a RAG corpus, a vector store or a hosted memory service taints every later session that reads that store; and *agentic execution*, where output drives tool calls (file system, shell, email, cloud APIs, MCP servers, sub-agents), so the blast radius reaches whatever the tools reach, and tool outputs re-enter the context, enabling chained or self-replicating effects.

An injection's anatomy runs along three axes (p. 10) [AR]: *delivery surface* (direct input, retrieved content, tool output, tool connection channel, persistent memory); *propagation behavior* (single-shot, multi-step kill-chain, cross-session through memory or RAG, self-replicating across agents); and *encoding* (plain text, base64 or other obfuscation, invisible Unicode, multimodal or steganographic, low-resource language). Decomposing a scenario along these axes is a threat-modeling step before choosing mitigations (p. 10) [AR].

Severity varies with the business context and the agency the model is given; outcomes include disclosure of sensitive information, system-prompt content, retrieved private documents or infrastructure details; manipulated output that downstream systems or users act on; unauthorized tool invocation escalating to arbitrary command execution and destructive actions where the agent has shell, file-system or cloud-API access; exfiltration via image-URL channels, hidden Unicode in rendered output, or covert tool-logging side channels; and persistent compromise across sessions through memory or RAG poisoning (pp. 10–11) [AP]. The entry concerns the input boundary itself: what the model leaks through outputs, including reasoning-channel content, is LLM02; the consequences of output reaching privileged actions are LLM03; output sanitization is LLM10 (p. 11) [AP].

**Types of prompt injection.** *Direct:* a user, or an attacker with the user's access path, supplies input that changes behavior; it can be intentional (a malicious user crafting a jailbreak) or unintentional (a legitimate user pasting content that happens to carry conflicting instructions, or a user who relies on an LLM and inadvertently optimizes input against an unrelated downstream LLM, as in Scenario #3) (p. 11) [AP]. Jailbreaking is the subset aimed at making the model violate its safety protocols; application-level safeguards help contain it, but effective prevention requires ongoing updates to the model's training and safety mechanisms (p. 11) [AR].

*Indirect:* the model ingests content from an external source (web page, document, email, tool response, RAG passage, image, MCP server output, database row, issue title) whose data acts as injection; the user neither supplied nor saw those instructions (p. 11) [AP]. The delivery surface's trust profile decides which defenses are practical (pp. 11–12) [AR]: *untrusted* surfaces (public web pages, unknown-sender email, search results), which defenders must treat as suspicious and where most research has focused; *semi-trusted* surfaces (issue titles in a public bug tracker, package READMEs and changelogs, third-party API responses), content the user chose to retrieve but did not author; and *trusted* surfaces (the developer's own repositories, databases, internal documents and mail), where the developer may not realize an attacker has placed content, perhaps via an unrelated upstream vector such as a public bug-report form.

The shared structure: the attacker need not compromise the backend; they place text where the developer's LLM will read it, and the LLM, holding the developer's privileges, does the work. "Defenses that focus only on the chat surface miss this entirely." [V] (p. 12) [AR]. Indirect injection increasingly turns the user's own LLM against the user's own backend: the attacker submits text through a low-privilege channel (a public form, a customer ticket, a community pull request) and waits for the user's MCP-connected agent or developer assistant to read it under elevated credentials. "The agent, not the attacker, performs the privileged action" [V] (p. 12) [AR].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 12–13) [AE]:
1. Direct prompt-input override of the system prompt's role and capability limits; intentional and unintentional inputs both count.
2. Indirect injection through retrieved content (a RAG passage, web page, document or email), for example EmailGPT (INCIBE-CERT, 2024) [BT].
3. Trusted-surface indirect injection: text planted in an issue tracker, feedback form or support ticket makes the user's LLM act under its elevated credentials, exfiltrating repositories, dumping databases or modifying IDE config (Invariant Labs, 2025; General Analysis, 2025; Rehberger, 2025a) [BT].
4. Multimodal and steganographic injection: sub-perceptual perturbations in images, audio or video extracted by the encoder (Clusmann et al., 2025) [BT].
5. Invisible-character injection and exfiltration through tag-block, variation-selector and zero-width Unicode; the August 2024 M365 Copilot ASCII-smuggling proof of concept exfiltrated a Slack MFA code (Rehberger, 2024) [BT].
6. Cross-session memory and RAG corpus poisoning: one tainted entry reaches every future session that reads it (W. Zou et al., 2025) [BT].
7. Fine-tuning interface as gradient oracle ("fun-tuning"): per-example loss read from a vendor's fine-tuning API optimizes a payload, with 65% to 82% attack success on Gemini, bringing white-box-style optimization to closed-weight models (Labunets et al., 2025) [BT].
8. Multilingual, encoded or low-resource-language payloads raise attack success and evade classifiers not trained on the scheme; Base64, ROT13 or emoji encodings bypass filters that never saw them (Hackett et al., 2025) [BT].

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies.** Prompt injection is "intrinsic to current generative AI" [V]: LLMs do not separate instructions from data and behave stochastically, so "no reliable prevention mechanism exists today" [V], a position the entry calls consistent with NIST (2025), NCSC (2025) and Debenedetti et al. (2025) (p. 13) [BT]. "Defense is therefore architectural rather than interceptive." [V] Design the surrounding system on the explicit assumption that the instruction boundary will eventually be bypassed, and constrain what the model may do and what its outputs may reach, so a successful injection does not become a successful exploit (p. 13) [AR].

Most high-impact injection incidents on record became severe because the injection landed in a system whose tools, scopes or output rendering let the compromised model act for the attacker at the user's privilege level (Scenarios #7–#9); injection is the input-side compromise, and excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy (LLM03) give it consequences outside the chat window (p. 13) [AR]. Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" (2025) restates this as a pre-deployment check: an agent that can at once access private data, ingest untrusted content and communicate externally has the conditions for high-impact exploitation, and removing any one leg removes them (p. 13) [BT].

The controls are defense-in-depth, since no single one suffices. Some reduce injection success and are expected to degrade against adaptive attackers; others bound the blast radius once injection succeeds, and those survive attackers who can probe the system. For agentic deployments the least-privilege and capability-budgeting controls (#4, #8) are "load-bearing" [V], and LLM03 carries the agency-side treatment (p. 13) [AR]. Each control carries its stated limit (pp. 13–15) [AP]:

1. Constrain the model's role and capabilities in the system prompt with declarative allow and deny statements, not open-ended grants. Partial only: an attacker who infers the prompt can bypass it (Nasr et al., 2025), so pair it with #4 (p. 13).
2. Define a strict output schema and validate every response in trusted application code before any downstream action, using structural validation rather than a second LLM call. It catches format violations, not semantic manipulation: a schema-valid response can still carry a malicious SQL query or an exfiltration-formatted email body (p. 14).
3. Filter at every modality boundary: modality-specific classifiers, OCR over images, transcription over audio, then text filters on the extracted content. Semantic filters are evadable by rephrasing or encoding, and low-resource and code-mixed inputs degrade them (Hackett et al., 2025) (p. 14).
4. Hold credentials and state-change capability in application code, not the model; grant least privilege per operation; route privileged calls through a deterministic policy engine that re-validates intent and arguments at execution time. NIST AI 100-2 E2025 and the CISA and Five Eyes OT joint guidance (CISA et al., 2025) frame such deterministic mediation as a baseline procurement expectation; broad "convenience" permissions and multi-agent hops re-introduce the risk downstream (p. 14) [BT].
5. Strip tag-block (U+E0000 to E007F), variation-selector (U+FE00 to FE0F) and zero-width (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060) characters at every ingest and render boundary; variation-selector variants smuggle arbitrary bytes invisibly (Rehberger, 2025c). Stripping does not stop visible-text payloads or future steganographic classes (p. 14).
6. Pass external content through a structurally separate, provenance-labeled channel so the model can tell data from instructions (S. Chen et al., 2025; Microsoft Research, 2025). This reduces attack success in non-adaptive tests only: an attacker who knows the marking scheme can mimic it, and StruQ was bypassed under adaptive attack (Nasr et al., 2025) (p. 14) [BT].
7. Require explicit human confirmation before any privileged, irreversible or externally visible action, showing the reviewer the exact rendered action, not a summary. Invisible-character smuggling can make the displayed action differ from the executed one, and "approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgment at volume" [V] (p. 14).
8. Budget agent capabilities with the Rule of Two as a floor (Meta AI, 2025): treat simultaneous access to (A) untrusted input, (B) sensitive data and (C) state change or external communication as high-risk; any [A,B,C] agent needs per-action human approval, and [A,B] or [A,C] configurations need an explicit residual-risk assessment. NIST AI 100-2 E2025 and the CISA, FBI, NSA and ACSC OT guidance endorse the rule, which is silent on autonomy depth (Noma Security, 2025) (p. 14) [BT].
9. Treat agent memory writes as privileged: log the causing prompt, classify writes for instruction or role-modification content, and require approval before instruction-bearing memories persist across sessions. A February 2025 Gemini proof of concept (Rehberger, 2025b) poisoned memory via delayed tool invocation (MITRE, n.d.). Factual entries shade into instructions, and incremental writes can evade per-write classification (pp. 14–15) [BT].
10. Pin, sign and verify every MCP server and third-party tool package, audit tool descriptions for hidden instructions, and monitor tool composition, treating them as a software supply-chain surface (LLM04 for third-party tool packages; ASI04 for MCP servers and tool registries). Pinning does not stop a payload shipped in the pinned version, or tool-description poisoning that leaves the version unchanged (p. 15).
11. Test against adaptive attackers who have read the deployed defense, and reject static-only attack-success claims: baseline with AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024), then red-team with the full defense specification disclosed. Nasr et al. (2025) "found static attack success near zero while adaptive attack success exceeded 90% for most of 12 recent defenses" [V]; see also LLMail-Inject (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2025) (p. 15) [BT].

**Example Attack Scenarios** (pp. 15–17) [AE]. Each closes with an anatomy line: (a) delivery surface, (b) propagation, (c) encoding.
- #1 Direct Injection: a customer-support chatbot is told to ignore its guidelines, query private data stores and send emails, leading to unauthorized access and privilege escalation. (a) direct user input, (b) single-shot, (c) plain text (p. 15).
- #2 Indirect Injection via Retrieved Web Content: asked to summarize a page with hidden instructions, the model inserts a markdown image whose URL exfiltrates the private conversation; the user sees only the rendered image. (a) retrieved web content, (b) single-shot with image-URL exfiltration, (c) plain text hidden in page source (p. 15).
- #3 Unintentional Injection: a job-description PDF embeds an AI-detection instruction; an applicant unknowingly uses an LLM to optimize their resume against it, the model surfaces the instruction, and the recruiting system flags the candidate, "a prompt injection with neither party acting maliciously" [V]. (a) indirect (document/PDF), (b) single-shot, (c) plain text (p. 15).
- #4 RAG Repository Poisoning: poisoned documents in a retrieved corpus alter output; as few as five poisoned documents have reached roughly 90% attack success against a knowledge base of millions of texts (W. Zou et al., 2025) [BT]. (b) cross-session / cross-user (pp. 15–16).
- #5 Payload Splitting: instructions split across resume fields (header, body, attachment) so no field looks malicious to a per-field classifier; the LLM recombines them at evaluation and its recommendation is manipulated (p. 16).
- #6 Multimodal Steganographic Injection: an instruction embedded below the human visual threshold is extracted by a vision encoder, producing harmful output or an unauthorized tool call; demonstrated against four frontier vision-language models in oncology imaging (Clusmann et al., 2025) and against general-purpose models via combined visual perturbation and text steering (R. Chen et al., 2025) [BT] (p. 16).
- #7 Zero-Click Document-Borne Agentic Exfiltration: a crafted email triggers a productivity assistant to exfiltrate organizational data with no user interaction; Aim Security demonstrated it against Microsoft 365 Copilot (Reddy & Gujral, 2025), bypassing both the deployed prompt-injection classifier and the link-redaction filter. (c) plain text with an invisible-Unicode exfiltration channel (p. 16) [BT].
- #8 Agentic Destructive Command Execution: two July 2025 events, different vectors, same class of impact. An attacker committed a destructive system prompt to the Amazon Q VS Code extension repository before AWS reverted it, though the committed code failed to execute because of a syntax error (Amazon Web Services, 2025a); separately, a runtime injection caused Amazon Q to execute arbitrary code (Amazon Web Services, 2025b). An agent with shell, file-system or cloud-API access amplifies an injection into a host-impacting incident (p. 16) [BT].
- #9 Trusted-Backend Indirect Injection through MCP: text planted in a public GitHub issue, a support ticket or a malicious npm package is read by the developer's LLM under elevated credentials. Invariant Labs (2025) exfiltrated private repositories via a poisoned GitHub issue; General Analysis (2025) dumped a production database through Cursor's Supabase MCP server running service_role and bypassing row-level security; the malicious postmark-mcp package (Koi Security, 2025; Toulas, 2025) BCC'd email to an attacker across an estimated 300 organizations. (b) multi-step tool-chain (pp. 16–17) [BT].

### LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure (pp. 18–22)

**Description.** Sensitive information disclosure occurs when an LLM-integrated system exposes confidential, regulated, privileged or proprietary data through a channel the data subject, controller or system owner did not authorize (p. 18) [AP]. The channel is not only the final answer: tool-call arguments, reasoning traces, retrieved chunks, multimodal output, logs, telemetry, embeddings, and observable inference properties (timing, token length, log-probabilities, confidence, cache-hit behavior) are all disclosure surfaces, each to be treated as an output under the same classification and redaction rules (p. 18) [AR].

Disclosure arises across four lifecycle phases (p. 18) [AP]: *training-time*, where a model, fine-tune or LoRA adapter memorizes corpus content and reproduces it verbatim or recoverably (memorization scales log-linearly with capacity, duplication and context length, and narrow adapters memorize rare examples with high fidelity, an extraction surface distinct from the base model); *inference-time*, where the model discloses live context (system prompt, RAG chunks, files, tool outputs, memory, another session's data), often because summarization, translation or extraction surfaces more than asked, including visually-redacted spans; *pipeline-time*, where fine-tuning, distillation, synthetic-data generation, gradients, SDKs and observability move sensitive data into derived artifacts; and *observation-time*, where adversaries infer facts from measurable properties (token length under TLS, latency, log-probabilities, confidence, cache-hit signals) without receiving content.

Protected information includes PII, PHI, financial data, credentials, API keys, trade secrets, model weights, privileged communications, classified or export-controlled material, and biometric and genomic identifiers (p. 18) [AP]. Two structural failures drive most incidents (p. 18) [AR]. *Oversharing upstream:* unscoped drives, legacy permissions and knowledge bases feed RAG with sensitive data the model then retrieves as designed; "The fix is the data surface, not the model" [V] (DSGAI01). *Persistence:* once data influences weights, embeddings or adapters, it stays extractable after source deletion, straining GDPR Article 17 and CCPA §1798.105 erasure obligations. Open-weights deployments cannot rely on rate limits, since extraction, membership inference and inversion run offline at unbounded rates (p. 18) [AR].

"Severity should turn on what the recipient can learn, not on whether the leak looked like natural language." [V] (p. 19). Applicable regimes include the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, high-risk obligations from August 2026), GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, ISO/IEC 42001 and NIST AI 600-1 (p. 19) [AP]. The entry covers the LLM as an application component; where it acts as an autonomous actor (cross-session memory, tool choice, multi-step exfiltration), the amplified risk is owned by ASI, with deeper controls in DSGAI (p. 19) [AP].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 19–20) [AE]:
1. Training-data memorization and extraction: the November 2023 "poem" divergence attack drove gpt-3.5-turbo to emit more than 10,000 unique memorized examples for roughly USD 200 (Nasr et al., 2023) [BT]; vendor patches have been bypassed repeatedly; fine-tuned models and their LoRA adapters are more extractable than base models of the same scale; litigation exhibits in NYT v. OpenAI and Getty v. Stability AI include verbatim reproduction, the Getty case centred on watermark reproduction (p. 19).
2. Inference-time context and output disclosure: the March 2023 ChatGPT Redis bug exposed payment PII for 1.2% of Plus subscribers; more than 4,500 shared conversations were indexed by Google in 2025 through missing noindex directives; clinical-embedding vector stores sit in a HIPAA audit-control scope most teams have not operationalized, and retrieval-layer authorization is widely under-implemented. "Treat reasoning traces and tool arguments as outputs, not debugging leftovers." [V] The trace channel also enables reasoning-trace-coercion model extraction; regex and blocklist filters fall to cross-lingual, base64 and hex encodings; aggregation across individually-permitted sources (budget + hiring + diligence → a pending M&A target) is a disclosure when policy prohibits the synthesized conclusion (p. 19).
3. Embedding and representation disclosure: modern inversion reconstructs plaintext from leaked or exported vectors, so an "embeddings-only" backup is a source-document breach. "Cosine similarity does not respect ACLs." [V] Authorize before retrieval, because post-generation filtering cannot undo a chunk already supplied to the model; the mechanisms belong to LLM09 and DSGAI13, and this entry owns the regulatory consequence (p. 19).
4. Multimodal disclosure: vision models OCR credentials and PII from screenshots, notifications and PDF metadata; generators reproduce watermarks and identifiable faces, "the Getty / Stable Diffusion watermark case is canonical" [V]; cross-modal transformation (text rendered as image, image OCR'd to text) bypasses single-modality DLP (p. 19).
5. Inference-time side channels: SPV-MIA raised membership-inference AUC to 0.9 against fine-tuned targets (Fu et al., 2024), enough for a regulatory breach determination about a named individual; Whisper Leak (McDonald & Bar Or, 2025) classified conversation topics at greater than 98% AUPRC across 28 production models from encrypted traffic; Weiss et al. (2024) reconstructed 29% of response content and inferred topic for 55% via token length; Wu et al. (2025) showed prompt leakage through KV-cache sharing in multi-tenant serving; Dong et al. (2025) inverted a 4,112-token medical prompt from a middle layer at an F1 of 0.8688 (token matching); Carlini et al. (2024) recovered a production model's projection layer through a logit-bias channel (pp. 19–20) [BT].
6. Training-pipeline disclosure: gradient inversion by a malicious server (Boenisch et al., 2021), distillation and synthetic-data carryover move examples into derived models; iterative query attacks against a DP-protected model refine LLM-generated queries and home in on confidence spikes to re-identify individuals, so fixed-epsilon DP is necessary but not sufficient without rate-limiting, query-pattern detection and per-user budgets (p. 20) [BT].
7. Platform and ecosystem disclosure: observability platforms (Langfuse, LangSmith, Datadog LLM Observability) log full prompts, completions, chunks and traces by default. Two representative incidents: DeepSeek's January 2025 ClickHouse exposure of more than one million rows of logs and API keys (Wiz, 2025), and Check Point's 2026 disclosure of ChatGPT exfiltration through a hidden outbound channel in the code-execution runtime, where one crafted prompt turned the runtime into a silent DNS channel while the visible answer stayed benign (Check Point Research, 2026) (p. 20) [BT].

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies.** Mitigations follow the DSGAI tiered structure as a graduated implementation path (p. 20) [AP].

*Tier 1: Foundational (every deployment)* (p. 20) [AP]: govern corpora (provenance, classification, deduplication across near-duplicates, transliterations and format variants; scrub PII at ingest; deduplication reduces but does not eliminate memorization); minimize context (send only task-required fields to external providers; disable auto-context such as customer_360 or full-record append unless justified per template); authorize before retrieval (document- and chunk-level authorization inside the index query, not at the application layer after retrieval; per-tenant indexes for high-sensitivity workloads); system-prompt hygiene (never store secrets, credentials or regulated data in system prompts); sanitize with classifiers, not regex alone (pattern matching plus NER plus trained classifiers, since regex fails on encoded and cross-lingual output); budget queries per user and session on sensitive endpoints; operational hygiene (restrict and scrub logs and traces before APM ingestion, encrypt in transit and at rest, and technically enforce no-train/no-retain rather than policy text alone).

*Tier 2: Hardening (regulated / high-sensitivity)* (pp. 20–21) [AP]: DP-SGD calibrated to sensitivity and cardinality, with overfitting monitored as a memorization proxy and paired with detection, because fixed budgets degrade under adaptive querying; vector-store protection (encryption, ACLs separate from document ACLs, restricted export APIs, minimum-scope k-NN, embedding-space probing detection); gate log-probabilities, confidence and explanations on production endpoints; classify and redact reasoning traces as first-class output and never log raw traces to unrestricted observability; side-channel defenses (random padding and token batching for streaming, high-sensitivity tenants on dedicated prefix caches, partitioned KV caches under co-tenancy); format-preserving encryption for structured identifiers, with internal-versus-external routing separation and field allowlists on the external path; AI-aware audit logging into SIEM, continuous DLP and AI-SPM, and a documented domain inventory with an enforced join policy so individually-permitted sources cannot combine into prohibited conclusions.

*Tier 3: Advanced (regulated, classified, high-target)* (p. 21) [AP]: confidential computing (Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, AWS Nitro Enclaves) or emerging privacy-preserving inference (the AloePri covariant-obfuscation framework, Lin et al., 2026) where the threat model justifies the utility and latency cost; verifiable erasure across raw data, embeddings, checkpoints and adapters, validated by post-unlearning extraction and membership-inference probes; disclosure red-teaming as a release gate (extraction, membership inference, embedding inversion, internal-state inversion, side channels, LoRA extractability), measured quantitatively and aligned to MITRE ATLAS; auditing synthetic data against extractors, resisting distillation with probing detection, rate limits and watermarking, and budgeting aggregate analytics; and exercising a disclosure incident-response playbook: scope by data class and affected subject or session, then assess and meet breach and serious-incident notification obligations across regimes (for example GDPR, HIPAA and EU AI Act Article 73), followed by unlearning, retraining or withdrawal, vector and cache cleanup, vendor notice and a persistent-memory audit.

**Example Attack Scenarios** (pp. 21–22) [AE]: #1 divergence prompts make a production model emit memorized PII, URLs and live credentials at scale, triggering GDPR Article 33 notification; #2 a shared-inference-state defect leaks one user's medical-letter prompt into another user's reasoning trace, and HIPAA 60-day notification applies; #3 extended-thinking traces logged verbatim to a shared APM project expose retrieved PII to hundreds of engineers while the answer stays sanitized; #4 prompt injection makes a support bot print its system prompt and an embedded vendor API key; #5 a shared legal RAG index crosses firm boundaries, synthesizing one client's privileged strategy into another's answer, an attorney-client waiver event; #6 a leaked "embeddings-only" vector backup is reclassified as a source-document breach after inversion, restarting the 72-hour clock; #7 Whisper Leak topic inference on encrypted streaming identifies users querying medical, legal or political topics without decryption; #8 membership inference against a clinical fine-tune identifies training-set patients at high AUC without extracting any record, a HIPAA-reportable determination; #9 a model summarizes PII hidden beneath a black-rectangle PDF redaction layer rendered over unmodified text; #10 an injected "diagnostic check" makes a code runtime encode spreadsheet content into DNS queries while the visible statistical summary stays benign.

(2024); Boenisch et al. (2021); Wiz (2025); Check Point Research (2026); Lin et al. (2026); DSGAI (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2026, data security v1.0); the NYT v. OpenAI and Getty v. Stability AI cases, without a reference entry. The reference list (pp. 110–111) adds: BeyondScale (2026) on vector database security; The Guardian (2026), "Anthropic Claude Code source leak"; InstaTunnel (2026) on differential privacy reversal via LLM feedback; C. Jiang et al. (2024) on feedback-guided extraction of a knowledge base from RAG applications; Lakshmanan (2026) on a Claude extension flaw enabling zero-click XSS prompt injection; Panda et al. (2024), "Teach LLMs to phish"; Unit 42 (2026) on Gemini Live in Chrome hijacking (CVE-2026-0628).

### LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency (pp. 23–26)

**Description.** Developers often grant an LLM-based system agency: the ability to call functions or interface with other systems via tools (also called extensions, plugins or skills by different vendors) to act in response to a prompt; an agent may choose its tool dynamically from the prompt or prior output, and agent systems typically make repeated LLM calls, using earlier outputs to ground and direct later ones (p. 23) [AP]. "Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction." [V] (p. 23). Common triggers are hallucination/confabulation from poorly-engineered benign prompts or a poorly-performing or misaligned model, and direct or indirect prompt injection from a malicious user, an earlier invocation of a malicious or compromised tool, or, in multi-agent systems, a malicious or compromised peer agent (p. 23) [AP].

The root cause is typically one or more of excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy (p. 23) [AR]. Impacts span confidentiality, integrity and availability, depending on which systems the app can reach; in agentic systems Excessive Agency can manifest as ASI02 Tool Misuse & Exploitation, ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse and ASI08 Cascading Failures (p. 23) [AP]. It differs from Improper Output Handling, which concerns insufficient scrutiny of outputs; sanitization of inputs and outputs "is not a root control for Excessive Agency" [V] and belongs to LLM01 and LLM10 (p. 23) [AR].

**Common Examples of Risk** (p. 24) [AE]: (1) *Excessive Functionality*: a tool includes functions the system does not need, e.g. a document-reading need met by a third-party tool that can also modify and delete; (2) *Excessive Functionality*: a tool trialled during development and dropped for a better alternative stays available to the agent; (3) *Excessive Functionality*: an open-ended tool fails to filter instructions outside the intended operation, e.g. a tool to run one specific shell command that does not prevent others; (4) *Excessive Permissions*: a read tool connects with an identity that also holds UPDATE, INSERT and DELETE; (5) *Excessive Permissions*: a tool meant to act in an individual user's context uses a generic high-privileged identity, e.g. reading the current user's documents through an account with access to all users' files; (6) *Excessive Autonomy*: the app fails to independently verify and approve high-impact actions, e.g. deleting a user's documents without confirmation.

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (pp. 24–26) [AP]. Actions that prevent Excessive Agency:
1. *Minimize tools*: offer only the tools needed; no URL-fetching tool if the system does not need one (p. 24).
2. *Minimize tool functionality*: a mailbox-summarizing tool may need only to read, so it should not delete or send (p. 25).
3. *Avoid open-ended tools* (run a shell command, fetch a URL) in favour of granular ones; writing output to a file through a shell tool leaves "the scope for undesirable actions" [V] very large, so build a specific file-writing tool; tools should define a strict schema for input parameters and validate contents before use (p. 25).
4. *Minimize tool permissions*: an agent making product recommendations might need only read access to a 'products' table, enforced through the database permissions of the identity the tool uses (p. 25).
5. *Execute tools in the user's context*: track user authorization and scope so actions run downstream in that user's context with minimum privileges (e.g. OAuth with minimum scope); in delegated or multi-agent workflows, preserve the original user context and authorization scope across chained tool or agent calls rather than relying only on the calling agent's or service identity's permissions (p. 25).
6. *Require user approval*: human-in-the-loop approval for high-impact actions, in a downstream system or within the tool, e.g. an approval routine inside a social-media 'post' operation (p. 25).
7. *Complete mediation*: "Implement authorization in logic rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not." [V] All requests to downstream systems are validated against security policies by the tool, by an independent pre-execution policy decision point between tool and downstream system, or by the downstream system itself, which also helps where an agent's nominally-permitted action is contextually unsafe. A graduated enforcement policy (audit, warn, block, escalate) lets low-consequence or easily reversible actions auto-approve while high-consequence or irreversible ones go to human review: a chatbot can auto-process a refund as store credit, which is recoverable, while an external payout routes to human approval (pp. 25–26).

Options that "will not prevent Excessive Agency but can limit the level of damage caused" [V] (p. 26): 8. *Monitor tool use*: log and monitor tools and downstream systems to find undesirable actions and respond. 9. *Rate limiting*: thresholds on tool invocation, with circuit breakers that halt, rate-limit or escalate to human review; simple thresholds count invocations, context-aware thresholds track the cumulative value of a tool's input parameter (p. 26).

**Example Attack Scenario** (p. 26) [AE]. The entry gives one. *#1 Hijacked Email Assistant:* a personal-assistant app reads a user's mailbox through a tool to summarize incoming email, but the chosen tool can also send. A crafted incoming email (indirect prompt injection) makes the LLM command the agent to scan the inbox for sensitive information and forward it to the attacker. It could be avoided by eliminating excessive functionality (a read-only mail tool), excessive permissions (OAuth with a read-only scope), and/or excessive autonomy (the user manually reviews and hits 'send' on every drafted mail); rate limiting the mail-sending interface could reduce the damage.

**References named.** The entry body cites no works. Its reference list (p. 112) names: Bort (2026), TechCrunch, on a Meta AI security researcher who said an OpenClaw agent ran amok on her inbox; Ferreira (2026), Tom's Hardware, on Claude Code deleting developers' production setup, including its database and snapshots ("2.5 years of records"); Kovacs (2026), SecurityWeek, on Google addressing Vertex security issues after researchers weaponized AI agents; Kundel (2024), Twilio, "Rogue agents"; Lucas (2024), NVIDIA, on sandboxing agentic workflows with WebAssembly; Meta AI (2025), "Agents rule of two" (also cited in LLM01); NVIDIA (n.d.), NeMo-Guardrails interface guidelines; Rehberger (2023), on a ChatGPT plugin exploit from prompt injection to private data.

### LLM04:2026 Supply Chain (pp. 27–32)

**Description.** LLM supply chains are susceptible to vulnerabilities affecting the integrity of training data, models, adapters, conversion pipelines and deployment platforms, resulting in biased outputs, security breaches or system failures (p. 27) [AP]. Where traditional software risk centres on code flaws and dependencies, in ML the risks extend to third-party pre-trained models, datasets and model artifacts, which can be tampered with, poisoned or maliciously replaced (p. 27) [AR]. Building LLMs depends on third-party models, datasets and reusable adapters built with PEFT techniques such as LoRA and shared on platforms like Hugging Face; the supply chain now includes model artifacts, provenance and conversion/merge workflows as first-class attack surfaces, and on-device LLMs widen it (p. 27) [AR]. Some of these risks also appear in LLM05, which this entry covers from the supply-chain side; agentic supply-chain risks, including MCP servers and tool registries, belong to ASI04 (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2026), and MITRE ATLAS catalogs the adversary techniques under AML.T0010 AI Supply Chain Compromise (MITRE, n.d.) (p. 27) [BT]. Figure 3 is captioned as a simple LLM supply-chain threat model illustrating supply-chain attack surfaces (p. 28) [AP].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 28–29) [AE]:
1. *Vulnerable or outdated third-party components and models* (packages, serving frameworks, models), similar to A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components but riskier when used in model development, fine-tuning or inference. LLM coding assistants hallucinate plausible but nonexistent package names at scale (Spracklen et al., 2025), which attackers register in advance ("slopsquatting") so unverified AI-suggested dependencies resolve to malicious code (p. 28) [BT].
2. *Licensing risks*: diverse software and dataset licences impose different usage, distribution and commercialization terms, creating legal and compliance exposure if unmanaged (p. 28).
3. *Vulnerable or tampered pre-trained models*: artifacts are hard to inspect comprehensively, and "static analysis alone cannot establish behavioral safety" [V]. A model can carry hidden biases or backdoors from poisoned datasets or direct tampering. Moving away from unsafe serialization such as Python pickle, which can execute arbitrary code on load, reduces but does not remove the risk: a backdoor can sit in the computational graph and persist in formats widely considered safe, such as ONNX, and a crafted model file can exploit memory-corruption bugs in a format's native parser, as with heap overflows in llama.cpp's GGUF parsing (CVE-2024-23496) (Cisco Talos, 2024) (p. 29) [BT].
4. *Weak provenance and unsigned model artifacts*: Model Cards document a model but do not prove its origin, and a compromised or lookalike supplier account can publish under a trusted name; unsigned or un-hash-pinned models, adapters, datasets, checkpoints and conversion outputs can be replaced or silently altered in transit, in storage, or at the promotion boundary where pipelines accept artifacts into trusted environments, especially when they resolve a mutable reference (for example, a latest tag) instead of an immutable digest (p. 29).
5. *Vulnerable adapters and compromised conversion, merge and quantization workflows*: a malicious LoRA adapter can compromise the base model in collaborative merge environments or on inference platforms that download and apply adapters; conversion and merge services can introduce malicious changes, bypassing review; weights can be crafted so the full-precision model evaluates benignly while the quantized artifact shows attacker-chosen behavior (Egashira et al., 2025), so full-precision assurances do not transfer to the deployed quantized artifact (p. 29) [BT].
6. *On-device LLM supply-chain vulnerabilities*: compromised manufacturing, device OS or firmware exploits, and re-packaged apps with tampered models make device integrity and firmware trust part of the LLM supply chain (p. 29).
7. *Unclear T&Cs and data privacy policies* of model operators can lead to application data being used for training and later exposed, and may create copyright risk from supplier material (p. 29).

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (p. 30) [AP]:
1. Vet data sources and suppliers, including T&Cs and privacy policies; use only trusted suppliers; review and audit supplier security and access regularly, and re-assess when their security posture or T&Cs change.
2. Apply the OWASP Top Ten A06:2021 mitigations (vulnerability scanning, management, and a patching policy keeping components, APIs and models on maintained versions), extend them to development environments with access to sensitive data, and verify that AI-suggested dependencies exist and are the intended package before adopting them.
3. Apply AI red teaming and evaluations when selecting third-party models, focused on in-scope use cases, and continue in production with anomaly detection and adversarial robustness testing in MLOps and LLM pipelines.
4. Keep an up-to-date, signed inventory via an SBOM extended to models, adapters and datasets with AIBOMs and ML SBOMs (options include the OWASP CycloneDX ML-BOM and the OWASP AIBOM project), tracking licences in the same inventory and auditing it regularly.
5. Use only models from verifiable sources and compensate for weak provenance with third-party integrity checks, signing and file hashes. Cryptographic model signing backed by a transparency log (the OpenSSF Model Signing project and Sigstore) binds an artifact to a signer identity (Open Source Security Foundation, 2025); reproducible builds are not guaranteed for model training, and CoSAI provides a maturity model for signing ML artifacts (OASIS Open, 2025). "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety" [V]: a validly signed model from a compromised or trusted-but-malicious supplier can still be backdoored, so combine signing with immutable artifact references, provenance policy, policy-based release gates (for example, SLSA), behavioral evaluation and continuous validation of upstream model integrity; use code signing for externally supplied code [BT].
6. Monitor and audit collaborative model development environments, and treat model conversion and merge services as high-risk promotion points.
7. Encrypt edge-deployed models with integrity checks, use vendor attestation APIs against tampered apps and models, and reject unrecognized firmware and untrusted device states.

**Example Attack Scenarios** (pp. 31–32) [AE]:
- #1 Compromised Packages and Serving Frameworks: in the December 2022 PyTorch supply-chain attack, a malicious torchtriton package on PyPI shadowed the PyTorch-nightly dependency and exfiltrated data (PyTorch Foundation, 2022). The serving stack is the same attack surface: the ShadowRay attacks exploited the disputed CVE-2023-48022 (unauthenticated dashboards on production Ray servers) in the wild, later escalating into a self-propagating botnet across exposed clusters (Lumelsky & Elbaz, 2025); in Ollama, CVE-2024-37032 allowed remote code execution through a malicious model manifest pulled from a registry (Wiz, 2024) (p. 31) [BT].
- #2 Tampered Model Published to a Hub: the PoisonGPT proof of concept spread misinformation through surgically modified parameters while evading standard benchmark evaluation (Huynh & Hardouin, 2023); the same trust gap covers fine-tunes that strip a model's safety features while keeping benign performance (Zhan et al., 2023), any pre-trained model deployed without verification, and shared AI-as-a-service platforms where researchers escaped an inference container via a malicious model to reach other customers' models and data (Tamari & Tzadik, 2024) (p. 31) [BT].
- #3 Compromised Supplier LoRA Adapter: an attacker infiltrates a supplier and alters a LoRA adapter later merged into a deployed LLM, giving a covert entry point (p. 31).
- #4 Hijacked Model Conversion or Merge Service, as in HiddenLayer's research on hijacking the Safetensors conversion bot on Hugging Face (HiddenLayer, 2024) (p. 31) [BT].
- #5 Model Namespace Reuse: a model referenced only by its Author/ModelName identifier; the original author deletes or transfers the account, an attacker re-registers the name and publishes a malicious model, and pipelines and managed catalogs that resolve by name pull it, leading to remote code execution (Saraf & Balassiano, 2025) (p. 31) [BT].
- #6 Scanner, Safe-Loader and Safe-Format Bypass: corrupted or compression-wrapped pickle streams execute before the scanner reaches the broken byte, as in the nullifAI models on Hugging Face (Zanki, 2025); scanners and safe-loader flags have had CVE-assigned bypasses, such as the PickleScan zero-days (Cohen, 2025) and torch.load with weights_only (CVE-2025-32434) (GitHub Security Advisories, 2025); a ShadowLogic-style backdoor in the computational graph (Wickens et al., 2024) of a "safe" format like ONNX attaches no executable code for a scanner to flag. Treat scanners and safe-loader flags as defense-in-depth layers, not guarantees, alongside provenance verification and patched loaders and parsers (p. 32) [BT].
- #7 Compromised Build Pipeline for Model Artifacts: an attacker compromises the CI/CD pipeline that fine-tunes and publishes models (a malicious build-workflow dependency, a stolen artifact-registry credential, cache poisoning), as in the Ultralytics attack, where GitHub Actions cache injection published trojanized PyPI releases of a flagship AI library, including a compromised "fix" release (Python Package Index, 2024). The entry calls this the same build-time substitution as the xz-utils backdoor and the Codecov breach; because the artifact is built and signed by the organization's own release infrastructure, it passes downstream provenance checks, internal attestation and scanners that flag only externally sourced components (p. 32) [BT].
- #8 Reverse-Engineered Mobile App: an attacker replaces the on-device model with a tampered version that leads users to scam sites and distributes the re-packaged app through social engineering (p. 32).
