### LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning (pp. 33–37)

**Description.** Data and Model Poisoning is a class of attacks and failures in which an adversary, or an unsafe process, manipulates data or model artifacts to embed harmful behavior, bias or exploitable weaknesses (p. 33) [AP]. It is not limited to training data: it can occur wherever data is ingested, transformed, retrieved or reused, including pre-training, fine-tuning, embedding creation, RAG and model distribution, and the resulting system may still appear functional while behaving in ways that undermine trust, safety and security (p. 33) [AR]. Data poisoning, intentional or unintentional (poor data hygiene, contaminated sources), makes the model learn the wrong patterns, internalize malicious correlations or behave incorrectly, with harmful outputs, impaired capabilities and degraded reliability (p. 33) [AP]. Poisoning targets the model's learning process, not a single runtime bug; unlike software flaws patched by fixing code, it can require data revalidation, retraining, model replacement or pipeline redesign, which is expensive and operationally disruptive (p. 33) [AR].

The stages named are pre-training (contaminated corpora), fine-tuning (domain-specific failure modes or hidden triggers), embeddings and vectorization (poisoning targets stored vectors to influence retrieved content, resulting in steered answers or subtle misinformation), transfer learning and model reuse, and continuous learning pipelines, where automated ingestion without validation lets attackers shape behavior gradually (p. 33) [AP]. The surface expands as organizations rely on external datasets, RAG pipelines, shared repositories and agentic workflows; shared-repository models carry risk through bundled non-weight artifacts (malicious deserialization such as pickle files, and tampered chat templates, tokenizer configs, LoRA/PEFT adapters and quantization artifacts), any of which can execute harmful code or alter behavior when loaded. Such backdoors may leave behavior untouched until a trigger, "creating the opportunity for a model to become a sleeper agent" [V] (p. 34) [AR]. In agentic deployments poisoning extends to tool integrations, persistent memory stores and RLHF feedback loops, covered in depth in the Agentic Top 10 (p. 34) [AP]. The entry covers durable corruption of persistent data or model behavior; instructions delivered through retrieved content at inference time belong to LLM01, and attacks exploiting embedding geometry to LLM09 (p. 34) [AP].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 34–35) [AE]: (1) training and fine-tuning data poisoning, including a targeted variant that erodes refusal behaviors while preserving general accuracy, undetectable through standard evaluation; (2) financial model data poisoning, with mislabeled transactions teaching a fraud model to label fraud as legitimate; (3) open-source dataset supply-chain poisoning, where trigger phrases in a shared dataset propagate into many downstream fine-tunes and force costly retraining once discovered; (4) low-volume high-impact backdoor poisoning: as few as 250 poisoned documents compromise models from 600M to 13B parameters regardless of dataset size (Souly et al., 2025) [BT]; (5) AI recommendation or memory poisoning through hidden instructions in web content; (6) RAG knowledge-base poisoning: a single optimized poisoned text per targeted query can override accurate content, keeping high success against paraphrasing, instructional-prevention and detection-based defenses (Zhang et al., 2025) [BT]; (7) agent and multi-system poisoning across AI-driven ecosystems; (8) healthcare model poisoning, where minimal poisoning of medical training data alters outputs while passing standard evaluations; (9) malicious AI models in the supply chain, whose downloaders inherit hidden triggers or system compromise (p. 35).

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (pp. 35–36) [AP]: (1) track dataset and model lineage with SBOM/ML-BOM (e.g. CycloneDX), enforce signing and verification, and continuously validate data integrity; (2) strictly validate incoming data, vet third-party vendors, and compare outputs against trusted sources; (3) protect RAG with trust boundaries, filtering of retrieved content, source scoring and isolation of system instructions from external data; (4) sandboxing and strict isolation from unverified data, tools and systems; (5) statistical and AI-based anomaly detection across training, embedding and inference, monitoring training loss, outputs and behavior for drift against defined thresholds; (6) curated domain-specific fine-tuning datasets; (7) least-privilege access, network segmentation and strict data access controls; (8) data version control (e.g. DVC) for rollback and forensic analysis; (9) control automated retraining and feedback loops by validating incoming data, requiring human oversight and rate-limiting against gradual poisoning through manipulated preference signals; (10) continuously red team with adversarial inputs and trigger-based prompts: "Do not assume safety alignment removes backdoors." [V] Dedicated trigger-probing is required after every alignment cycle (Hubinger et al., 2024) [BT]; (11) grounding techniques with validation layers so retrieved content is verified before influencing outputs (p. 36); (12) treat inference artifacts (chat templates, tokenizer configs, LoRA/PEFT adapters, quantization artifacts) as security-relevant code, with signing, hash verification, diff checks and static analysis before deployment (p. 36).

**Example Attack Scenarios** (pp. 36–37) [AE]: #1 manipulated documents in an internal knowledge repository surface in responses, leading to incorrect recommendations, manipulated business decisions or reputational damage; #2 hidden instructions in webpages summarized by AI tools, once ingested into RAG or memory, bias the model to recommend specific products; #3 crafted inputs to an automated retraining feedback loop, needing only standard user-interface access, cause slow drift toward degraded accuracy, bias or unsafe recommendations; #4 a malicious insider injects mislabeled transactions and the model fails to detect fraud; #5 poisoned pre-trained weights uploaded to a public repository survive standard safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024) [BT]; #6 a chat template modified (for example in a GGUF package or tokenizer config) with trigger-activated conditional instructions behaves normally under benign inputs; validated across 18 models and 4 inference runtimes, factual accuracy drops from 90% to 15% under trigger conditions and URL emission exceeds an 80% success rate (Fogel et al., 2026) [BT]; #7 loading a third-party model with unsafe serialization (e.g. pickle) executes embedded code, enabling host compromise and lateral movement (p. 37); #8 in a shared AI environment one tenant injects adversarial data into shared embeddings or memory, contaminating other tenants' responses; #9 malicious instructions injected into an agent's persistent memory over multiple sessions make it prioritize attacker-controlled logic, with long-term workflow manipulation and hidden persistence (p. 37).

**References named.** In the entry body: Souly et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025); Hubinger et al. (2024); Fogel et al. (2026); CycloneDX and DVC as examples. The reference list (p. 114) adds: F5 (2025), a data and model poisoning guide to the 2025 OWASP list; GitHub (2026), an advisory on server-side template injection in Giskard Agents (GHSA-frv4-x25r-588m); JFrog Security Research (n.d.), GGUF-SSTI; MITRE (n.d.), ATLAS; NIST (2023), AI RMF 1.0.

### LLM06:2026 Unbounded Consumption (pp. 38–42)

**Description.** Unbounded Consumption occurs when an LLM application allows excessive and uncontrolled inferences, letting attackers disrupt availability, inflict unsustainable costs or steal intellectual property through model cloning, by exploiting the absence of adequate controls over resource consumption (p. 38) [AP]. The high compute demands of LLMs, particularly in cloud and pay-per-token environments, make them inherently susceptible (p. 38) [AR]. "A defining characteristic of this threat is cost asymmetry." [V] Attackers trigger disproportionately expensive computation at negligible cost to themselves, through crafted prompts, stolen credentials or manipulated workflows (p. 38) [AR]. The risk is compounded by extended-thinking and reasoning models with large or insufficiently constrained output budgets, multimodal models with higher per-request compute, agentic architectures and tool-use protocols such as MCP that amplify a single request into cascading downstream operations, and shared inference infrastructure. "Traditional request-rate limiting alone is no longer sufficient." [V] Defense needs token-aware cost controls, hard spending caps, agent-level circuit breakers and continuous cost-attribution monitoring (p. 38) [AR].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 38–39) [AE]:
1. Variable-length input flood and output explosion, including output explosion via fine-tuning poisoning, where a single malicious training sample breaks end-of-sequence behavior and pushes output to maximum length on every request (Gao et al., 2024) (p. 38) [BT].
2. Denial of Wallet (DoW): a high volume of operations exploits the cost-per-use model, imposing unsustainable costs on the provider (p. 38).
3. Large-context abuse: since many APIs reject over-limit inputs outright, the durable risk comes from requests that stay just within limits while inflating per-request cost (p. 39).
4. Reasoning-loop and thinking-token exhaustion: short, benign-looking prompts force extended-thinking models into prolonged or non-terminating reasoning, bypassing input-size filters (Li et al., 2025); standard input validation gives no protection (p. 39) [BT].
5. Adversarial inputs optimized for resource overconsumption, including sponge examples (Shumailov et al., 2020) and adversarial visual perturbations, using gradient-based and gradient-free optimization over the input space (p. 39) [BT].
6. Multimodal inputs and outputs convert into large token counts; overhead varies with model, provider, resolution, media duration and preprocessing (p. 39).
7. Model extraction and distillation theft: crafted queries collect enough outputs to replicate a partial model or fine-tune a functional equivalent; exposed logits and log-probabilities accelerate extraction (Carlini et al., 2024); side-channel extraction of weights or architecture belongs to LLM02 (p. 39) [BT].
8. Agent-tool interactions flooding resources: published tools force an application into recursive or infinite tool-calling loops, and when one call fans out, the LLM may need to manage "hundreds of calls spawned from a single task" [V] (p. 39).
9. Inference infrastructure exploitation of serving frameworks (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, Triton, Ollama) through unsafe deserialization, special-token injection and injected chat templates (p. 39).

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (pp. 40–41) [AP]: (1) rate limiting and input-size validation, moving beyond requests per second to tokens-per-minute, tokens-per-day and estimated cost per request, with pre-flight token estimation to reject requests before inference; (2) hard spending caps: non-overridable budget ceilings per API key, user, team and cloud account that halt inference, "rather than alerting thresholds that fast-accumulating workloads can outpace" [V], accounting for modality and tool-protocol cost differences; (3) dynamic resource allocation management; (4) sandboxing access to network resources, internal services and APIs, limiting exfiltration of extracted model information; (5) graceful degradation under heavy load; (6) limits on queued and total actions, with dynamic scaling and load balancing; (7) scanning inputs, particularly visual inputs to LVLMs, for adversarial perturbations; (8) detecting resource-intensive tool interactions by monitoring for recursive actions without a clear end state and baselining normal tool token consumption; (9) agentic circuit breakers: step, recursion-depth and time limits and per-run cost ceilings on every agent execution, with state hashing to detect recursive loops (p. 41); (10) inference infrastructure hardening: updated serving frameworks, unsafe deserialization disabled, special-token passthrough restricted, authentication on all inference endpoints (p. 41).

**Example Attack Scenarios** (pp. 41–42) [AE]: #1 uncontrolled input size; #2 repeated requests making the service unavailable to legitimate users; #3 resource-intensive queries prolonging GPU use; #4 Denial of Wallet; #5 functional model replication by fine-tuning another model on synthetic data generated through the API; #6 adversarial image perturbations that make an LVLM overconsume output tokens (Gao et al., 2025) [BT]; #7 multi-turn tool-calling loops and fan-out: a published malicious tool (e.g. via a Claude Skill on an open-source repository) instructs an agent into recursive cyclical tasks or many tool calls, and developers who incorporate it risk excessive token consumption and instability (pp. 41–42); #8 growing context in agentic sessions: an attacker or a benign user keeps a session open and gradually adds content, so each inference re-processes the whole context; per-turn cost climbs from roughly $0.001 on the first turn to about $0.50 by turn 100, no single request triggers rate limits, and the aggregate across many concurrent or long-lived sessions reaches hundreds of dollars (p. 42).

**References named.** In the entry body: Gao et al. (2024, 2025); Li et al. (2025); Shumailov et al. (2020); Carlini et al. (2024). The reference list (pp. 114–115) adds: Akkus (2024) on extracting AI models from mobile apps; Anthropic (n.d.), Vision documentation; Awan (2023) on watermarking; DeepLearning.AI (2023) on the LLaMA leak; B. Dong et al. (2026), "Clawdrain", on tool-calling chains for stealthy token exhaustion in OpenClaw agents; W. Jiang et al. (2024) on defending against model extraction; moohax & monoxgas (2023), Proof Pudding (CVE-2019-20634); Nevo et al. (2024), RAND, on securing AI model weights; Radosevich & Halloran (2025), an MCP safety audit; Sev (2023), Sourcegraph, on unauthorized admin access; Taori et al. (2023), Alpaca.

### LLM07:2026 Misinformation (pp. 43–45)

**Description.** Misinformation occurs when an LLM or LLM-enabled application produces incorrect, incomplete, unsupported or misleading information that appears credible enough to influence a human decision, an automated workflow or an agent action. "The core risk is that the incorrect output is trusted and acted upon." [V] (p. 43) [AR]. Because model outputs now drive tool calls, generate code, infer system state, authorize actions and coordinate across agents, "This makes misinformation a system-level failure" [V] that can lead to financial loss, security incidents, safety risks or operational disruption; in agentic systems it often appears as incorrect state, reasoning or evidence consumed downstream, leading directly to unintended actions (p. 43) [AR].

It can arise from hallucination, incomplete or stale context, weak grounding, ambiguous prompts, biased or corrupted data, misleading summaries or unvalidated tool outputs, and it can be deliberately induced (p. 43) [AP]. Where the root cause is prompt injection, poisoning or supply-chain compromise, those risks are referenced separately; the execution of unsafe generated code is LLM10, and registering hallucinated package names is LLM04. This entry covers the resulting failure mode: a false representation that drives a harmful decision or action (p. 43) [AP]. Overreliance remains a key factor: humans and systems treat fluent, confident or well-structured outputs as authoritative, and "In agentic architectures, this overreliance is frequently embedded in system design." [V] (p. 43) [AR].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 43–44) [AE]: (1) unsupported or false decision support influencing business, legal, healthcare, financial or operational decisions; (2) incorrect state inference in workflows, where the model infers a condition has been met when it has not; (3) incorrect or fabricated code and dependencies, including hallucinated packages (Spracklen et al., 2025) [BT]; (4) misleading summaries and critical omissions of constraints, exceptions, timestamps or risks; (5) adversarially induced misinformation; (6) cross-agent misinformation propagation; (7) forged or misattributed evidence presented as authoritative (p. 44).

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (p. 44) [AP]: (1) ground claims before action in authoritative and current sources; (2) Claim-Check-Act patterns that separate generation from execution and verify claims before acting; (3) validate tool calls: arguments, authorization, preconditions and current state before execution; (4) use verification signals, not just confidence: groundedness and consistency checks; (5) runtime verification for high-impact actions through approval workflows and system checks; (6) detect and prevent omission failures with structured outputs carrying mandatory fields; (7) limit blast radius with least privilege, sandboxing and rate limits; (8) monitor and test: log claims, evidence and outcomes, and test adversarial scenarios; (9) calibrate human and system trust by distinguishing verified facts from assumptions; (10) adversarial evaluation and continuous testing against misleading scenarios.

**Example Attack Scenarios** (p. 45) [AE]: #1 a coding assistant recommends a plausible but nonexistent package an attacker has pre-registered, and a trusting developer installs attacker-controlled code (Spracklen et al., 2025) [BT]; #2 a customer-service agent misreads a policy and approves a refund that violates the terms; #3 a clinical summary omits a drug contraindication and a clinician acts on the incomplete recommendation; #4 an attacker seeds a support forum with false remediation steps that a troubleshooting agent retrieves and repeats as a trusted recommendation; #5 a security agent misclassifies normal traffic as an intrusion and automatically blocks a production network segment, causing an outage; #6 a retrieval agent reports a customer as identity-verified when they are not, and a downstream payment agent trusts that state and releases funds; #7 fabricated task completion: an agent reports a nightly database backup completed when it never ran, and a later restore fails because no backup exists.

**References named.** In the entry body: Spracklen et al. (2025). The reference list (p. 116) adds: NIST (2024), AI 600-1; OpenAI (2025), "Why language models hallucinate"; OWASP Gen AI Security Project (2025), LLM09:2025 Misinformation; W. Zou et al. (2025), PoisonedRAG.

### LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure (pp. 46–49)

**Description.** Hidden Context Exposure is the unauthorized extraction, inference or reconstruction of hidden, non-user-facing system instructions or operational context placed in a model's context; it becomes security-relevant when that context contains or reveals secrets, policy logic, tools, trust boundaries, workflow criteria, proprietary behavior or other implementation details that materially increase attacker capability (p. 46) [AP]. Hidden context typically includes the system prompt, developer instructions, retrieved policy text (from RAG knowledge bases, configuration stores or user-profile services), the schemas of tools and functions exposed to the model, and other rules and materials assembled into the context window: not meant for end users, but accessible to the model (p. 46) [AP].

"Practitioners should design under the assumption that hidden context is discoverable and that any contents of the context should not be considered a secret." [V] Developers should make disclosure carry little or no direct security impact: no credentials, connection strings or tokens in hidden context, and no reliance on it alone as a security boundary for authorization, privilege separation, policy enforcement or content filtering (p. 46) [AR]. Severity tracks what is placed there and how the application relies on it: *informational* (no secrets, no security-relevant logic, no reliance on confidentiality); *medium* (internal rules, filtering criteria, role descriptions or workflow logic that aids an attacker but does not gate critical decisions); *high* (embedded credentials or tokens, or reliance on hidden-context secrecy for authorization or content policy); *critical* (disclosure chains to remote code execution, broad data exfiltration or privilege escalation in a connected system) (p. 46) [AR]. It also amplifies adjacent categories: disclosed rules enable targeted injection (LLM01); embedded credentials are sensitive information disclosure (LLM02); revealed tool permissions and schemas expand excessive agency (LLM03); leaked output-formatting rules can facilitate improper output handling (LLM10) (p. 46) [AR].

LLM08 covers the foundational risk that hidden control context is exposed, inferred or reconstructed in a way that materially increases attacker capability. It does not cover leakage of regulated user or training data (LLM02); agentic amplifications such as persistent memory, inter-agent channels, tool configuration persistence and multi-step agent compromise (the Agentic Top 10); or generic application-security concerns such as server-side log leakage, client-side bundle inspection and infrastructure-layer side channels (p. 47) [AP].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 47–48) [AE]: (1) exposure of sensitive functionality, tool and function schemas (system architecture, tools, API keys, database credentials, user tokens), where "the real risk is that sensitive credentials are placed in the hidden context in the first place" [V]; (2) exposure of behavioral control logic, giving insight into how to exploit weaknesses or bypass controls; (3) reverse engineering of safety and refusal mechanisms: where a user sees only "Sorry, I can't do that," leakage reveals the triggers, conditions and exceptions behind it, letting attackers craft inputs that avoid known refusal patterns or exploit gaps in enforcement; (4) disclosure of permissions and user roles, e.g. a tool description from an internal-facing MCP server saying a user must have the developer role, inviting probing through directed conversation and injection (LLM01) and possibly revealing more (LLM02); (5) exposure of output structure and formatting rules (JSON schemas, templates, validation constraints), letting attackers produce format-conforming responses with manipulated values that lead to incorrect parsing or unintended behavior (p. 48).

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (p. 48) [AP]: (1) *do not put sensitive data in hidden context*: assume all context available to the LLM is available to users, and externalize secrets and security-critical configuration to systems the model does not directly access; (2) *use deterministic methods and guardrails*: hidden context should not be the primary control on model behavior; specialized fine-tuning may reduce disclosure risk but gives no consistent guarantee and may have unintended consequences; enforce critical behaviors through independent, deterministic systems outside the model, e.g. harmful-content detection by external safeguards; (3) *enforce authorization and access control independently from the LLM*: privilege separation and authorization bounds checks must not be delegated to the LLM, but enforced deterministically and auditably, "which LLMs are not well suited to provide" [V]; separate tasks by authorization context, each with only the privileges it needs.

**Example Attack Scenarios** (p. 49) [AE]: #1 a system prompt holding tool credentials is leaked and the attacker uses the credentials for other purposes; #2 conversational probing extracts the tool list and parameter schemas; no credential leaks and no policy is overtly bypassed, but the attacker gains concrete targets for later prompt injection and reconnaissance for downstream action chaining; #3 a system prompt prohibiting offensive content, external links and code execution is extracted and used to craft an injection that bypasses those restrictions.

**References named.** The entry body cites no works. Its reference list (p. 116) names: Cao et al. (2025) on mitigating prompt leakage via system vectors; Das et al. (2025) on system prompt extraction attacks and defenses; Goffin (2025), Resk, a proof of concept on the dangers of system prompt leakage; Hui et al. (2024), PLeak; jujumilk3 (2025), a GitHub repository of leaked system prompts; LeakHub (n.d.); Z. Li et al. (2025) on system prompt poisoning; Nie et al. (2024), LeakAgent; Zheng et al. (2026), "Just ask: Curious code agents reveal system prompts in frontier LLMs".

### LLM09:2026 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (pp. 50–54)

**Description.** These weaknesses arise in any LLM application that turns text, images, code or audio into numerical representations and uses similarity search to decide what the model sees; RAG is the familiar case, and the same machinery underlies vector-backed agent memory, semantic caches and deduplication pipelines. Whenever similarity search sits between a data source and the prompt, the embedding layer becomes part of the application's trust boundary (p. 50) [AR]. They are distinct from prompt injection: they exploit the geometry of the embedding space and the mechanics of similarity search, and many succeed when the retrieved content carries no malicious instructions at all (p. 50) [AR]. "A useful frame: poisoning makes the system wrong, inversion makes it leak, jamming makes it silent, and access-control failure makes it indiscriminate." [V] (p. 50). The entry covers attacks that depend on the embedding layer; indirect injection through retrieved content is LLM01, training-time poisoning of the embedding model is LLM05, serialization flaws in vector-store libraries are LLM04, and agent-memory attacks that do not rely on geometry are ASI06:2026 Memory and Context Poisoning. Vectorless retrieval (BM25-only, LLM-native tree navigation) inherits the non-geometric risks but has no LLM09 attack surface (p. 50) [AP].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 50–52) [AE]:
1. *Cross-tenant leakage via shared similarity search*: in multi-tenant deployments search often runs across the full index before application-layer access control, so an attacker can infer the existence, topic and approximate volume of other tenants' documents from result counts, score distributions and timing without seeing them, even when every document is correctly tagged and every call authenticated. Conventional auth flaws in vector-DB software (CVE-2025-64513 in Milvus, a forged sourceID header bypassing authentication, CVSS 9.3; CVE-2025-69286 in RAGFlow, predictable token derivation enabling account takeover, CVSS 9.3) are out of scope but compound the geometric risk: since a vector-store leak is recoverable to source documents via inversion, an auth bug in a vector database carries higher consequence than the same bug in a document database or key-value store (pp. 50–51).
2. *Embedding inversion*: reported recovery runs from roughly 50–70% of words from sentence embeddings to 92% exact reconstruction of short 32-token inputs with Vec2Text (Morris et al., 2023), which trains an inversion model per encoder; ZSInvert (C. Zhang et al., 2025) and Zero2Text (Kim et al., 2026) work zero-shot, cross-domain and black-box, and remain effective against differential-privacy noise added at storage [BT]. Vector-database backups, embeddings shipped to third parties and embeddings exposed through misconfigured cloud storage should be treated as a leak of the underlying documents; under GDPR and similar regimes breach notification depends on risk to data subjects, and because embeddings can be inverted, that risk is real (p. 51).
3. *Retrieval-time data poisoning*: an attacker who can write to the corpus (public scraping pipelines, file uploads, partner feeds, compromised internal sources) crafts content whose embedding lands near a target query; published attacks reliably achieve high success with a handful of poisoned documents, even in corpora of millions and against black-box systems. Success needs two conditions at once, retrieval (geometric) and steering (generation), so defenders can intervene at either layer; MITRE ATLAS catalogs the class as AML.T0070 (RAG Poisoning) under the Persistence tactic (p. 51) [BT].
4. *Retrieval jamming*: a "blocker" document engineered to be retrieved for a specific query makes the LLM refuse or claim it lacks information; it carries no malicious instructions, exploiting retrieval mechanics and LLM safety behavior, and a single blocker generated by black-box optimization, without access to the target embedding model or LLM, suffices. It is an availability attack on the retrieval layer (p. 51).
5. *Membership inference via similarity search*: if raw similarity scores or distances reach the client, the index is a direct membership oracle with no LLM involved; with only generated answers, partial documents or perturbed queries can still reveal membership, which can itself be sensitive (p. 51).
6. *Semantic cache and deduplication poisoning*: content crafted to land just above or below the cosine-similarity threshold can poison a cache entry for all semantically equivalent queries, bypass deduplication with near-duplicates of poisoned content, or force legitimate content to be dropped as a duplicate. Wu et al. (2026) demonstrate semantic cache poisoning end-to-end across AWS, Azure and Alibaba deployments; Z. Zhang et al. (2026) show black-box key-collision attacks that use surrogate embedding models to engineer threshold-straddling vectors; all three failure modes are invisible to document-level controls (pp. 51–52) [BT].
7. *Multimodal embedding poisoning*: cross-modal encoders such as CLIP and ColPali put images, audio, code and text in one space, so an attacker can craft an image whose embedding sits near a sensitive text query; MM-PoisonRAG (Ha et al., 2025) and Poisoned-MRAG (Liu et al., 2025) demonstrate local and global poisoning, and "One Pic is All it Takes" shows a single image suffices for targeted and universal VD-RAG poisoning; the image looks unremarkable to a reviewer and text-based scanning misses it (p. 52) [BT].

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (pp. 52–53) [AP]:
1. *Permission and access control*: enforce tenant scoping inside the index query, not as a post-retrieval filter, and validate it server-side; "A client-supplied scope is a suggestion, not a control." [V] Authenticate embedding and similarity-search endpoints as first-class APIs with per-tenant rate limits; use physically separated indexes per tenant or trust zone for high-sensitivity workloads; apply access control at the chunk level, since a mostly-public document can contain a confidential paragraph (p. 52).
2. *Data validation, source authentication and provenance*: normalize content before embedding (strip zero-width characters, white-on-white text and Unicode homoglyphs at extraction); track provenance for every embedding (source, ingestion time, trust tier, pipeline version) so compromised batches can be invalidated; human review for externally sourced content bound for sensitive indexes; vet the embedding model, since a backdoored encoder corrupts the geometry of everything ingested (p. 52).
3. *Data segregation by trust tier*: mixed-trust content must not share an index without hard isolation; index-level segregation beats classification tags on a shared index because it removes the misconfiguration path (p. 52).
4. *Anomaly detection at ingest and retrieval*: flag new vectors unusually close to many common queries, the signature of retrieval-hijacking poisoning; watch for queries returning too many high-similarity matches, unusual embedding-endpoint volume (a precursor to query-based inversion) and clusters growing faster than expected; withhold raw similarity scores, add noise and diversification at ranking, and rate-limit endpoints that could serve as oracles. Cross-encoder re-ranking raises attack cost but does not replace provenance and ingest controls, since modern attacks target retrieval and ranking jointly (p. 53).
5. *Storage lifecycle controls*: delete embeddings within a bounded time of source deletion and verify with reconciliation audits; hold vector-database backups at the source documents' sensitivity tier; encrypt embeddings at rest with keys managed apart from the application layer; re-embed the corpus when rotating the embedding model, since heterogeneous embeddings create exploitable gaps; treat embedding-API keys as secrets, since a leaked key gives query access to the exact encoder (p. 53).
6. *Monitoring, logging and incident response*: immutable retrieval logs (tenant scope, query, returned IDs, similarity scores); monitoring for tenant-filter bypass attempts, cross-tenant anomalies and abnormal embedding-API consumption; incident-response playbooks that treat "embeddings only" leaks as source-data leaks for breach assessment and notification under GDPR Article 33 and analogous regimes (p. 53).

**Example Attack Scenarios** (pp. 53–54) [AE]: #1 a RAG system that scrapes public documentation and forums retrieves an attacker's posts engineered to land near internal queries such as "what is our Q3 revenue projection"; the same text pasted into a chat would have no effect, and the attack works only because of where the content sits in embedding space (p. 53); #2 in a shared vector index with application-layer tenant filtering, Tenant A's probing queries reveal through timing, result counts and score gaps the existence and approximate topic of Tenant B's content, building a map over many queries; real-world incidents in the category include CVE-2025-69286 (RAGFlow), where predictable token generation enabled cross-account compromise (pp. 53–54); #3 a cloud misconfiguration exposes a vector-database backup; the incident is first classed low-severity because "only the embeddings leaked", until a zero-shot inversion attack reconstructs a substantial fraction of the source content, including PII, without the original encoder, and the incident is reclassified as a source-document breach with notification obligations reassessed; the entry concludes that "embeddings only" is not a safe-harbor classification (p. 54).

**References named.** In the entry body: Morris et al. (2023); C. Zhang et al. (2025); Kim et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026); Z. Zhang et al. (2026); Ha et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0070; "One Pic is All it Takes" by title (the reference list gives Shereen et al., 2025). The reference list (pp. 117–118) adds: Chaudhari et al. (2024), Phantom; Y. Chen et al. (2025), ALGEN; Z. Chen et al. (2024), AgentPoison; H. Li et al. (2023) on sentence-embedding inversion; Shafran et al. (2025), "Machine against the RAG", on jamming RAG with blocker documents; Song & Raghunathan (2020) on information leakage in embedding models; Tan et al. (2025), RevPRAG; F. Wang et al. (2024), Astute RAG; Xue et al. (2024), BadRAG; W. Zou et al. (2025), PoisonedRAG.

### LLM10:2026 Improper Output Handling (pp. 55–57)

**Description.** Improper Output Handling is insufficient validation, sanitization and handling of LLM outputs before they pass downstream to other components and systems (p. 55) [AP]. "Since LLM-generated content can be controlled by prompt input, this behavior is similar to providing users indirect access to additional functionality." [V] It concerns unsafe use of output before it passes downstream, while LLM07 concerns output that is incorrect or misleading; input validation is LLM01 (p. 55) [AP]. Exploitation can result in XSS and CSRF in browsers and SSRF, privilege escalation or remote code execution on backends (p. 55) [AP]. Conditions that increase impact: excessive application privileges granted to the LLM; susceptibility to indirect prompt injection that can grant an attacker privileged access to a target user's environment; unvalidated inputs from third-party tools; missing context-specific output encoding (HTML, JavaScript, SQL); insufficient monitoring and logging of outputs; missing rate limiting or anomaly detection; terminal, log or IDE sinks that render output without neutralizing control characters such as ANSI escape sequences; and client renderers (browser, chat UI, IDE, terminal) that automatically fetch resources referenced in output (Markdown images, link previews, iframes), enabling exfiltration through outbound requests (p. 55) [AP].

**Common Examples of Risk** (pp. 55–56) [AE]: (1) output entered into a system shell or functions such as exec or eval, resulting in remote code execution; (2) JavaScript or Markdown returned to a user and interpreted by the browser, resulting in XSS; (3) LLM-generated SQL executed without parameterization, leading to SQL injection (p. 56); (4) output used to construct file paths without sanitization, risking path traversal; (5) content used in email templates without escaping, risking phishing; (6) ANSI escape sequences or other control characters written to a terminal, log viewer or IDE pane, enabling visual spoofing, clipboard hijacking (for example, OSC 52) or exploitation of terminal-emulator vulnerabilities (Rehberger, 2024b) [BT]; (7) a chat UI auto-rendering Markdown images or link previews, letting an attacker who controls part of the context exfiltrate conversation data via the image URL's hostname or query string (Rehberger, 2024a) [BT].

**Prevention and Mitigation Strategies** (pp. 56–57) [AP]: (1) "Treat the model as any other user, adopting a zero-trust approach" [V], and validate responses coming from the model to backend functions; (2) follow OWASP ASVS guidance on input validation and sanitization (OWASP, n.d.); (3) encode output back to users to block code execution by JavaScript or Markdown, per ASVS output-encoding guidance; (4) context-aware output encoding by destination (HTML encoding for web content, JavaScript encoding for browser script contexts); (5) parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database operations involving output; (6) strict Content Security Policies; (7) logging and monitoring for unusual output patterns; (8) sanitize control characters (ANSI escape sequences, BEL, OSC, backspace, carriage return) and other non-printable bytes before output reaches terminals, log files or other interpreting sinks, encoding them visibly where they must be preserved; (9) in client renderers (chat UIs, IDEs, email clients, mobile apps), prevent output from triggering automatic outbound requests: disable auto-rendering of Markdown images, link previews and iframes by default, and where rendering is needed, restrict fetches to an explicit allowlist of origins or proxy them through a server-side fetcher that strips data-bearing query parameters (pp. 56–57).

**Example Attack Scenarios** (p. 57) [AE]: #1 a chatbot's LLM passes its response without validation to a tool that also offers administrative functions for another, privileged LLM, causing the tool to shut down for maintenance; #2 a website summarizer meets a prompt injection that makes it capture sensitive content from the site or the conversation, encode it and send it, unvalidated, to an attacker's server; #3 a chat feature that crafts SQL deletes all tables when a user asks and the query goes unscrutinized; #4 a web app returns an unsanitized JavaScript payload, leading to XSS in a victim's browser; #5 LLM-generated marketing email templates carry malicious JavaScript to recipients with vulnerable email clients; #6 an application compiles and deploys LLM-generated code without human review or security testing, so insecure code reaches production and is exploited.

**References named.** In the entry body: Rehberger (2024a, 2024b); OWASP (n.d.), ASVS. The reference list (pp. 118–119) adds: diskordia (2025) on CVE-2025-32711 (EchoLeak); Klondike (2023), AI Village, on threat modeling LLM applications; MITRE (2026), CWE-116; OWASP (2026), AISVS C7 on model behavior, output control and safety assurance; Porat (2025) on LangGrinch in LangChain Core (CVE-2025-68664); PortSwigger (n.d.), a lab on exploiting insecure output handling; Rehberger (2025) on GitHub Copilot remote code execution via prompt injection (CVE-2025-53773), also cited in LLM01; Willison (n.d.), a Markdown-exfiltration tag archive.

## Part III: Appendix A, Related Framework Mappings (pp. 58–105)

### Purpose and how to read it (p. 58)

Appendix A consolidates the mappings from the ten entries to nine external frameworks and taxonomies, replacing the per-entry Related Frameworks and Taxonomies sections, removed "in favor of this single, version-pinned reference" [V] (p. 58) [AP]. The coverage matrix shows which frameworks map to each risk; the by-framework sections give the element mappings and why they apply. Mappings sit at each framework's coarse level (tactics, pillars/weaknesses, risk categories, control domains), every element is drawn from the pinned version listed in Framework Sources & Versions, and each cell shows the primary mappings plus the most relevant supporting ones (p. 58) [AP]. Legend: ● primary, "a central line of defense or description of the risk" [V]; ○ supporting, contributing but "not the center of gravity" [V]; — no applicable mapping (p. 58).

### The nine framework sections (pp. 59–105)

Each section defines its own primary/supporting split [AP]:
- *OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI), 2026, announced 2025-12-09* (pp. 59–63): "Relocated verbatim from the 2026 entries" [V], mapping each LLM risk to ASI risks; every element in this section is marked primary. For LLM08, ASI06 and ASI07 are pointers for the agentic amplifications the entry defers, each "not an equivalent risk" [V] (p. 62). For LLM10, the ASI02 mapping is marked a "2026 addition" [V], and the ASI09 mapping is a "Canonical crosswalk baseline mapping" [V] whose content match the appendix calls loose, since the entry's scenarios are machine-to-machine while ASI09 concerns deceiving a human operator (p. 63).
- *OWASP GenAI Data Security 2026 (DSGAI), v1.0 (2026-03-17)* (pp. 64–68): primary elements name the closest data-security peer; supporting elements the most relevant adjacent data risks (p. 64).
- *MITRE ATLAS, content v2026.06 (format-version 6.0.0)* (pp. 68–73): the adversary tactics (AML.TAxxxx) an attack exploiting the risk traverses; primary tactics carry the core adversary objective, supporting tactics the enabling steps (p. 68).
- *MITRE ATT&CK v19.1* (pp. 74–77): Enterprise tactics (TA IDs); primary marks the risk's central attack objective, supporting the adjacent stages (p. 74).
- *MITRE CWE 4.20* (pp. 78–83): the weaknesses that name each entry's root cause; primary captures the definitional weakness, supporting the top contributing failure modes (p. 78).
- *NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) v1.0, July 2024* (pp. 84–88): risk categories; primary names the core risk, supporting the secondary facets (p. 84). The LLM07 note glosses Confabulation as "NIST's term for confidently stated but false output" [V] (p. 87).
- *NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1) v1.0, 2023* (pp. 89–92): the Categories whose outcomes the risk most directly exercises, "primary" marking a near-verbatim fit and "supporting" a partial or governance-level fit (p. 89). There is no LLM10 row.
- *CSA AI Controls Matrix (AICM) v1.1 (2026-06-22)* (pp. 93–99): control domains; primary domains carry the core control, supporting domains add defense in depth (p. 93).
- *OWASP AIVSS (AI Vulnerability Scoring System) v0.8* (pp. 100–104): the Agentic AI Core Security Risks the entry can produce or feed, primary marking those it most directly enables; AIVSS then scores the severity of those agentic risks (p. 100). There is no LLM02 row.
- *Framework Sources & Versions* (p. 105) lists each framework's version and source URL.

## Part IV: Appendix B and back matter (pp. 106–122)

### Appendix B: LLM Application Architecture and Threat Modeling (pp. 106–107)

Apart from the page footers, the text layer carries only the appendix title (p. 106); p. 107 has no body text. Its substantive content is in images, not inspected under text-only scope.

### References (pp. 108–119)

References are grouped by risk entry and formatted in APA-7; a source cited by more than one entry appears in full under each, with an "[also cited in ...]" note (p. 108) [AP]. Each entry's list is summarized under that entry above.

### Acknowledgements, sponsors and supporters (pp. 120–122)

The 2026 list is "the work of dozens of contributors" [V] from the security and AI engineering communities, too many to name individually; the acknowledgements thank everyone who drafted, reviewed, debated, voted, tested an entry against a real incident, or refined a mitigation, and name the project leads and entry leads listed in the Structure line (p. 120) [AP]. The sponsors page says sponsors fund operational and outreach costs, that the project maintains a vendor-neutral and unbiased approach, that sponsors receive recognition but no special governance considerations, and that all project materials are community developed and released under open source and Creative Commons licences (p. 121) [AP]. Project supporters "lend their resources and expertise to support the goals of the project" [V] (p. 122).

- OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI), 2026: the list hands over to it where the model becomes an actor, and entries defer agentic amplifications to it; one of the nine mapped frameworks [BT] (pp. 7, 15, 19, 23, 27, 34, 47, 50, 59–63).
- OWASP GenAI Data Security 2026 (DSGAI): LLM02 follows its tiered mitigation structure and defers deeper controls to it; one of the nine mapped frameworks [BT] (pp. 18–20, 64–68).
- MITRE ATLAS, MITRE ATT&CK v19.1, MITRE CWE 4.20, NIST AI 600-1, NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1), CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 and OWASP AIVSS v0.8: mapped frameworks in Appendix A, cited neutrally [BT] (pp. 58–105). ATLAS techniques AML.T0010 and AML.T0070 are also named in the entries (pp. 27, 51), and AML.T0080.000 in LLM01's reference list for the MITRE citation on p. 15 (p. 109).
- NCSC (2025), NIST (2025, NIST AI 100-2 E2025) and Debenedetti et al. (2025): cited as consistent with the position that no reliable prevention mechanism for prompt injection exists; NIST AI 100-2 E2025 and CISA et al. (2025) cited for deterministic mediation and for endorsing the Rule of Two [BT] (LLM01, pp. 10, 13–14).
- Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" (2025): cited approvingly as a restatement of the structural diagnosis [BT] (LLM01, p. 13).
- Meta AI's Rule of Two (2025): adopted as a floor for capability budgeting; Noma Security (2025) cited for the rule's silence on autonomy depth [BT] (LLM01, p. 14).
- Nasr et al. (2025): cited for bypassing system-prompt constraints, StruQ, and most of 12 recent defenses under adaptive attack [BT] (LLM01, pp. 13–15).
- OWASP Top Ten A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components, OWASP ASVS, OWASP CycloneDX ML-BOM and the OWASP AIBOM project: other OWASP work drawn on for controls [BT] (LLM04, pp. 28, 30; LLM10, p. 56).
- OpenSSF Model Signing, Sigstore, CoSAI's signing maturity model and SLSA: cited for model signing and release gates [BT] (LLM04, p. 30).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Building a model that cannot be fooled as the security goal.* The leads' first sentence rejects it in favour of building the system around a model that will be fooled (p. 5).
- *Letting one year of incident data overturn practitioner judgment.* The data gets a quarter weight so it cannot rewrite the list on its own (p. 5).
- *New thin categories for new risks.* Rejected as splintering the list for no gain (p. 7).
- *Interceptive defense of prompt injection.* Defense is "architectural rather than interceptive" because no reliable prevention mechanism exists (LLM01, p. 13).
- *Static-only attack-success claims.* To be rejected in favour of testing against adaptive attackers who have read the defense (LLM01, p. 15).
- *Validation by a second LLM call.* Output validation should be structural, in trusted application code (LLM01, p. 14).
- *Leaving authorization to the model.* Authorization belongs in logic, a policy decision point or the downstream system, not in an LLM's judgment or a system prompt (LLM03, p. 25; LLM08, p. 48).
- *Hidden context as a secret or a security boundary* (LLM08, pp. 46, 48).
- *Sanitization as a root control for Excessive Agency* (LLM03, p. 23).
- *Authorization after retrieval, and client-supplied scope* (LLM02, p. 20; LLM09, p. 52).
- *Regex alone for sanitization; policy text alone for no-train/no-retain* (LLM02, p. 20).
- *"Embeddings only" as a low-severity or safe-harbor classification* (LLM02, pp. 19, 22; LLM09, p. 54).
- *Signing as proof of safety; scanners and safe-loader flags as guarantees* (LLM04, pp. 30, 32).
- *Assuming safety alignment removes backdoors* (LLM05, p. 35).
- *Request-rate limiting alone, and alerting thresholds in place of hard caps* (LLM06, pp. 38, 40).
- *Confidence alone as the verification signal.* The control reads "Use Verification Signals (Not Just Confidence)" (LLM07, p. 44).
